question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of a NxN Matrix Using Cofactor Expansion
question.problem:
Calculate the determinant of the matrix
$Z=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 5 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
We use the cofactor expansion along the first row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Z) & ={z}_{11}{C}_{11}+{z}_{12}{C}_{12}+{z}_{13}{C}_{13}+{z}_{14}{C}_{14} \\  & =1\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & ={C}_{11}-{C}_{13} \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ ∗ & -3 & 5 & 4 \\ ∗ & 4 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & -1 & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & ∗ & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & ∗ & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & ∗ & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =(0\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}|-(-2)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}|+0\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}|)-(0\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}|-0\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}|+0\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}|) \\  & =0+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}|+0-(0-0+0) \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =2((-3)\cdot 5-4\cdot 4) \\  & =2\cdot (-31) \\  & =-62\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Polynomial Forcing
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-{x}^{2}-x-1.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.
question.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $, and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma ,$  we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
(2\alpha x+\beta )+(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=-{x}^{2}-x-1
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
\alpha {x}^{2}+(2\alpha +\beta )x+(\beta +\gamma )=-{x}^{2}-x-1
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\alpha =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 2\alpha +\beta =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \beta +\gamma =-1\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\beta =1,\gamma =-2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-{x}^{2}+x-2.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}-{x}^{2}+x-2.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Non-Pivot Columns of a Matrix in Row Echelon Form
question.problem:
The row echelon form matrix $A$ is given below. What are its **non**-pivot columns?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that the pivots of a matrix in row echelon form are the first non-zero entries in each row of the matrix.

We can see that $A$ has $3$ pivots in the $1$st, $2$nd and $4$th columns:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the only non-pivot columns are the $3$rd and $5$th columns.

Therefore, the only non-pivot column is the $1$st column.

The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
question.problem:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 & -0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{21}+5\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|+5\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|+5|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-3-0)+5(-6-4) \\  & =3-50 \\  & =-47\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second  $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+1\cdot {C}_{22}+5\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+5\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|-5|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =(0-2)-5(-8-4) \\  & =-2+60 \\  & =58\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|=-47+58=11.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
question.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+1\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-2)-2(2-4) \\  & =-1+4 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-4)\cdot {C}_{22}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =(-4)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(2+3)+2(1+6) \\  & =-20+14 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 3-(-6)=12.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Determinant of a Triangular Matrix
question.problem:
Consider the matrices $A$ and $B$ given below. Find $det(A)-det({B}^{T}).$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ \sqrt{2} & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2.5 & 0.21 \\ 0 & 2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ \sqrt{2} & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}|=(-1)\cdot (-1)\cdot 2=2 \\ det(B) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2.5 & 0.21 \\ 0 & 2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|=1\cdot 2\cdot (-3)=-6\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $det({B}^{T})=det(B)=-6.$ 

Finally, we obtain

$$
det(A)-det({B}^{T})=2-(-6)=8.
$$

question.problem: Given that $D=-2I$, where $I$ is the $4\times 4$ identity matrix, what is the value of $det(D)?$

First, notice that

$$

$$

The determinant of a diagonal matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}| & =(-2)\cdot (-2)\cdot (-2)\cdot (-2)=16.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of a Matrix With Many Zeros
question.problem:
Find the determinant of the matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 1 & 19 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that the $3$rd column contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 1 & 19 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 1\cdot (-3)=-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
det(B)=-9.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Volume of an N-Dimensional Parallelepiped
question.problem:
Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

$$
a=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,c=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,d=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $a,$ $b,$ $c,$ and  $d:$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 4 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M:$

$$
V=|det(M)|
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. So, we have

$$
det(M)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 4 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}]=7\cdot 3\cdot (-1)\cdot 5=-105.
$$

Therefore, the volume is

$$
V=|det(M)|=|-105|=105.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Volume of an N-Dimensional Parallelepiped
question.problem:
Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

$$
a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,c=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10 \\ 0 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,d=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $a,$ $b,$ $c,$ and  $d:$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 7 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 5 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M:$

$$
V=|det(M)|
$$

Notice that the $1$st row of the determinant contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 7 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 5 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the $2$nd row of the $3\times 3$ determinant contains two zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =-2|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot 4\cdot (-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =8|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =8(-14+30) \\  & =128.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume is

$$
V=|det(M)|=|128|=128.
$$
